 During financial aid delays, students spent weeks seeking resolution from the University
 Students faced unanswered calls and contradictory information when getting help with financial aid
 The Financial Aid and Scholarship Services office is pictured in the ASU Student Services Building in Tempe, AZ, on Thursday, March 27, 2025.
 Pedro Rojo 
 By Emma Bradford 
 |
 November 4, 2026 | 9:04pm MST 
 As federal financial aid changes took effect, ASU students said the University's financial aid office was overwhelmed and unprepared for the deluge of issues. The transition left students scrambling to get their aid disbursed.
 The One Big Beautiful Bill Act that President Donald Trump signed on July 4, 2025 included significant changes to the federal financial aid system, including new eligibility requirements for aid programs, loan borrowing limits and fewer loan repayment options. 
 The U.S. Department of Education negotiated new rules to implement the student loan provisions, with changes beginning less than two months before the start of ASU's Fall 2026 semester, according to a University webpage .
 As a result of these changes, universities around the country scrambled to change their procedures to comply with the law.
 READ MORE: New federal law will force tough decisions for student loan borrowers 
 But for ASU students who depend on federal financial aid to attend the University, those changes became disruptions. In their view, the University didn't do enough to support them through the process.
 James Valicenti, a doctoral student studying behavioral health, said the University told him he needed to check his eligibility for Grad PLUS loans for the rest of his program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act eliminated those loans moving forward, offering exceptions for students who met limited qualifications.
 Luckily, he said in a written statement that he qualified to keep the loan. The problem was that his financial aid account in My ASU was simultaneously showing as $0 and displaying a "Loan Processing" message, yet nothing was applied to his tuition.
 Valicenti, like many others, took to Reddit to express concerns over his aid and the issues he was having with ASU Financial Aid .
 In a written statement, a University spokesperson said ASU was working to help students understand the federal changes and was providing resources and support.
 "We acknowledge the delays some students have faced may have real consequences and our team is working very hard to resolve outstanding inquiries as fast as possible. This is happening at universities from coast to coast after changes made by the federal government to student borrowing guidelines."
 The University moved the tuition payment date to Sept. 25, the spokesperson stated. Another spokesperson said in an October written statement that around 100 graduate students receiving individualized financial aid help had the deadline further extended.
 Still, Valicenti wasn't satisfied with how the University has handled the situation.
 "They had a year, they knew these changes were going down the pipeline," Valicenti said. "It wasn't like, 'Oh this may or may not happen.' No, it was going to happen, and they knew about this."
 What is going on with Financial Aid? 
 by
 u/Party-Highlight-9940 in
 ASU 
 Student testimonies
 Mikayla Piantanida, a senior studying elementary education, said the changes meant she no longer qualified for loans she had for the past three years. One of them was the Parent PLUS loan, which the One Big Beautiful Bill placed new restrictions on.
 Piantanida said she was able to find a separate loan outside ASU. All that she needed was for the University to sign off confirming she was a student and enrolled in classes.
 After six weeks of hearing nothing from the University and receiving pressing emails from the loan company, she said she tried to call ASU Financial Aid. Piantanida said that once the office picked up a week later, they told her she would need to wait another six weeks. 
 After a couple more weeks, Piantanida said she decided to go in person to ASU Financial Aid, where someone was able to help her.
 "It took about three months for me to finally get this one piece of paper signed in order to pay the tuition," Piantanida said.
 Abigail Tremp, a senior studying liberal studies, said she faced issues purely as a result of the delays in disbursement of her scholarships, rather than federal financial aid.
 Tremp started the process to fix one of her scholarships in June, but said she was met with unanswered calls and wrong answers from ASU Financial Aid.
 "Eventually, two months after I started that, I finally got it fixed," Tremp said. "It was only because I called and demanded to speak to someone higher up."
 Once they got involved, her scholarship disbursement was fixed the same day, she said.
 "It clearly wasn't a very hard issue," Tremp said. "It just required someone who knew what they were doing to actually take care of it."
 As for Tremp's second scholarship, she said the check was not mailed until August. She sent several emails to ASU Financial Aid throughout the month to fix it and never received a response to any of them. 
 Tremp said the scholarship was applied within two to three weeks, but that was longer than what ASU Financial Aid initially told her.
 As for Kennedi Reeder, a sophomore studying biomedical sciences, she was seeking help from ASU Financial Aid for an outside loan to cover an overdue balance from last year — separate from the federal changes. Reeder said certifying the loan took from the beginning of August to mid-September.
 However, when she looked over the certified loan, she realized the office put it for the wrong school year, and told her she had to redo the process, Reeder said.
 When dealing with ASU Financial Aid, the longest Reeder said she was willing to wait on hold was about two hours. She said she was not going to waste her day waiting for someone to pick up the phone, so instead she opted into the callback option 
 When Reeder got a call back, she said it was four or five days later.
 "It's really hard to get any help, because then they pick up the phone and you ask them questions, and half the time they're like, 'Well, I don't know,'" Reeder said. "What do you mean you don't know? That's your job. It's your job to know."
 Students propose solutions
 For the financial aid process to be fixed at ASU, Reeder said the University needs to hire more employees for the financial aid office and train them better on the possible questions they may be asked.
 "Hire students, hire alumni, they already know a lot of things about ASU — they went there for God's sake," Reeder said. 
 Valicenti said this is one of the existing problems with ASU Financial Aid, exacerbated by fallout from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act the University seemed unprepared for.
 "There's not enough financial aid counselors and not enough people that are taking the calls," Valicenti said. "ASU is just not allocating money to be able to accommodate this mass change that's happening."
 Tremp recommended improving the office's communications and call center to avoid giving out incorrect information.
 She criticized how the University supported students through the federal changes.
 "They really did a terrible job at communicating this to students," Tremp said.
